sections.title: 1. What this language is and what it is for

blocks.text: Python is a high-level general-purpose language with simple, readable syntax. Code blocks are indented rather than wrapped in curly braces, so a program looks almost like plain text.

items: Data analysis and machine learning — pandas, NumPy, scikit-learn, PyTorch.
Web backend — Django, Flask, FastAPI.
Automation — scripts, file handling, web scraping, bots.
Science and engineering — computations, visualization, image processing.

blocks.text: Python is slower than C++ and Java, but it wins on development speed. That is why it is popular where getting results quickly matters more than squeezing out the last milliseconds.

sections.title: 2. Installing and setting up the environment

items.title: Download Python
items.text: Open python.org/downloads and click Download Python 3.12 or newer. The site will detect your operating system automatically.

items.title: Run the installer
items.text: On the first screen, make sure to check “Add python.exe to PATH” — otherwise the python command will not be found in the terminal. Then click Install Now.

items.title: Verify the installation
items.text: Open a new terminal (PowerShell or Command Prompt) and run the commands below. If the version appears, you are all set.

items.title: Install an editor
items.text: VS Code works well: install it from code.visualstudio.com and add the Python extension by Microsoft. PyCharm Community Edition is another option.

blocks.text: On Windows, the python command may be unavailable if PATH was not refreshed. In that case use py --version or reinstall Python with the PATH checkbox enabled.
Create a folder called hello and a file hello.py inside it. Open it in your editor and write one line:
Let's break down each part of the program:

items.text: A comment. Python ignores everything that starts with a hash. Comments are for people, not for the computer.
The name of the built-in output function. It is already part of Python, so there is no need to import it.
Parentheses mean a function call. Whatever you put inside them is what gets printed.
A string — text in double quotes. Single quotes work too: 'Hello, world!'.

blocks.text: Indentation is part of Python's syntax. This program has none, but inside conditions and loops it is required. Use 4 spaces rather than a tab.

items.title: Open a terminal in the project folder
items.text: In VS Code that is Terminal → New Terminal. Or open PowerShell and change into the folder with cd.

items.title: Run the file
items.text: Run python hello.py. “Hello, world!” will appear on the screen.

items.title: Or press Run in the editor
items.text: In VS Code with the Python extension, click the ▶ triangle in the top-right corner to run the current file.

blocks.code:
cd C:\projects\hello
python hello.py
# Hello, world!

blocks.text: First, solidify the basics: variables and data types, if/else conditions, for and while loops, functions, lists and dictionaries. Then move on to modules, files and venv virtual environments.

sections.title: 1. What this language is and what it is for

blocks.text: JavaScript is a programming language that runs right in the browser. It makes pages interactive: it handles clicks, validates forms, loads data and updates the interface without a reload.

items: Frontend — React, Vue, Angular, Svelte.
Backend — Node.js, Express, NestJS.
Mobile apps — React Native and Capacitor.
Games and graphics — Canvas API, WebGL, Three.js.

blocks.text: Modern JavaScript (ES2015+) means let and const, arrow functions, promises and async/await. It is better to start with it than with old tutorials full of var.

sections.title: 2. Installing and setting up the environment

items.title: Nothing to install for the browser
items.text: Open any page, press F12 and switch to the Console tab — JavaScript is already running. This is the fastest way to try the language.

items.title: Install Node.js
items.text: Download the LTS version from nodejs.org. Node.js is needed to run JavaScript outside the browser and install packages with npm.

items.title: Verify the installation
items.text: In a new terminal run node --version and npm --version. Both commands should print a version number.

items.title: Install VS Code
items.text: For convenience, add the ESLint and Prettier extensions — they highlight errors and format your code.

blocks.text: Create a file hello.js and add this line:
Let's break the program down:

items.text: A comment until the end of the line. The browser and Node.js do not execute it.
The global console object. In the browser it is connected to the DevTools panel, in Node.js to the terminal.
The log method prints the value passed to it. The dot means accessing a property of an object.
A string literal. You can use double quotes, single quotes or backticks.
A semicolon ends the statement. JavaScript can insert it automatically, but writing it explicitly is safer.

blocks.text: There are two equally valid ways: in the terminal via Node.js or in the browser console.

items.title: Via Node.js
items.text: Open a terminal in the folder with the file and run node hello.js.

items.title: Via the browser
items.text: Connect the file to HTML with <script src="hello.js"></script> and open the page. Look at the result in the Console tab (F12).

items.title: Via DevTools
items.text: You can paste console.log("Hello, world!") directly into the console and press Enter.

blocks.text: Basics: let/const variables, data types, conditions, loops, functions, arrays and objects. Then DOM, events, fetch and asynchrony. After that, choose React or Node.js.

items.title: TypeScript — JavaScript with types
items.text: The next step for large projects and teamwork.

items.title: HTML/CSS — you can't build a page without them
items.text: The structure and styling of the interface that JavaScript brings to life.

items.text: A popular alternative to Node.js on the server.

sections.title: 1. What this language is and what it is for

blocks.text: C++ is a compiled language with manual memory management. A program is turned into machine code and runs very fast, which is why C++ is chosen where performance and control over resources matter.

items: Game engines — Unreal Engine, custom engines and physics.
Systems programming — drivers, utilities, embedded devices.
Graphics and computing — CAD, rendering, signal processing.
High-frequency trading and financial systems.

blocks.text: C++ is harder than Python: you need to understand types, pointers, references and object lifetimes. In return, that knowledge makes you stronger in any other language.

sections.title: 2. Installing and setting up the environment

items.title: Install a compiler
items.text: On Windows, MSYS2 is the easiest option: download it from msys2.org, run pacman -S mingw-w64-ucrt-x86_64-gcc and add the bin folder to PATH. Alternatively, use Visual Studio Community with the “Desktop development with C++” workload.

items.title: Verify the compiler
items.text: Open a new terminal and run g++ --version. The GCC version should be displayed.

items.title: Install VS Code
items.text: Add the C/C++ extension by Microsoft and Code Runner. For debugging, an extension that configures launch.json is useful.

blocks.text: If g++ is not found, check that the compiler's bin folder is added to the PATH environment variable and restart the terminal.
Create a file hello.cpp and copy this code into it:
Let's go through each line:

items.text: Includes the standard input/output library. This is where std::cout is declared.
The program's entry point. The main function returns an integer (int) and takes no arguments. Execution starts here.
std::cout is the output stream to the screen. The << operator sends the string to it, and std::endl adds a newline and flushes the buffer.
Returns 0 — the success code. The operating system understands that the program finished without errors.
Closes the body of main. Every opening curly brace must have a closing one.

blocks.text: In C++, semicolons are required at the end of statements. They are not used after #include or after a block in curly braces.

items.title: Compile the program
items.text: In a terminal in the folder with the file, run g++ hello.cpp -o hello.exe. The -o flag sets the name of the resulting file.

items.title: Run it
items.text: On Windows run .\hello.exe, on Linux and macOS run ./hello.

items.title: Or use VS Code
items.text: Press F5 or the Run button. VS Code will call the compiler itself if the C/C++ extension is installed.

blocks.text: Basics: data types and variables, conditions, loops, functions, arrays and strings. Then move on to pointers and references, structs, classes and the STL standard library (vector, string, map).

items.title: C — the foundation of systems programming
items.text: No classes or STL, but as close to the hardware as it gets.

items.title: Rust — a safe alternative to C++
items.text: The same speed, but the compiler checks memory usage.

items.title: C# — games in Unity
items.text: An easier path into gamedev if C++ feels too hard for now.

sections.title: 1. What this language is and what it is for

blocks.text: Java is a strongly typed object-oriented language. Code is compiled to bytecode and runs on the JVM, so one program works on Windows, Linux and macOS without being rewritten.

items: Enterprise backend — Spring Boot, microservices, banking systems.
Android — classic apps (Kotlin is the modern alternative).
Big data — Hadoop, Spark, Kafka.
Desktop and server applications with reliable typing.

blocks.text: Java is more verbose than Python, but its strictness helps in large teams: errors are caught at compile time, and the library ecosystem is enormous.

sections.title: 2. Installing and setting up the environment

items.title: Install the JDK
items.text: Download JDK 21 (LTS) from adoptium.net. It includes not only the runtime but also the javac compiler.

items.title: Verify the installation
items.text: In a new terminal run java -version and javac -version. The versions should match.

items.title: Configure JAVA_HOME
items.text: Some tools look for the JAVA_HOME variable. Set it to the path of the JDK folder, for example C:\Program Files\Eclipse Adoptium\jdk-21.

items.title: Install an IDE
items.text: IntelliJ IDEA Community Edition is the most convenient free option. VS Code with the Extension Pack for Java also works.

blocks.text: Create a file Hello.java. The file name must match the public class name and is case-sensitive.
Let's go through each line:

items.text: Declares the public class Hello. In Java all code lives inside classes, and the file name must match the class name.

The main method is the entry point. public makes it accessible from outside, static allows calling it without creating an object, void means it returns nothing, and String[] args is the array of command-line arguments.
System.out is the standard output stream. println prints the string and moves the cursor to a new line.
The closing braces end the main method and the Hello class. Keep your braces balanced.

blocks.text: If you name the file hello.java in lowercase, the compiler will report: class Hello is public, should be declared in a file named Hello.java.

items.title: Compile
items.text: Run javac Hello.java. A Hello.class file with bytecode will appear next to it.

items.title: Run
items.text: Run java Hello — without the .class extension. “Hello, world!” will appear on the screen.

items.title: Or run it in the IDE
items.text: In IntelliJ IDEA, click the green triangle next to the main method.

blocks.code:
javac Hello.java
java Hello
# Hello, world!

blocks.text: Basics: data types, conditions, loops, methods, arrays. Then classes, inheritance, interfaces, collections (List, Map, Set) and exception handling. After that you can dive into Spring Boot or Android.

items.title: Kotlin — a modern language for Android
items.text: Compatible with Java, but shorter and safer.

items.title: C# — a similar path into .NET and Unity
items.text: Familiar OOP concepts in another ecosystem.

items.title: SQL — data for the backend
items.text: Java services almost always work with a database.

sections.title: 1. What this language is and what it is for

blocks.text: C# is a modern object-oriented language from Microsoft for the .NET platform. It is strict yet convenient: automatic garbage collection, a rich standard library and excellent IDE support.

items: Games — Unity, where C# is the main scripting language.
Web — ASP.NET Core, Blazor, Web API.
Desktop apps — WPF, WinUI, MAUI.
Cross-platform services and cloud solutions on .NET.

blocks.text: Modern .NET 8 runs on Windows, Linux and macOS. C# is similar to Java but adds properties, LINQ, async/await and more convenient syntax.

sections.title: 2. Installing and setting up the environment

items.title: Install the .NET SDK
items.text: Download the .NET 8 SDK from dotnet.microsoft.com/download. The SDK includes the compiler and project templates.

items.title: Verify the installation
items.text: In a new terminal run dotnet --version. The command should print a version, for example 8.0.400.

items.title: Install an editor
items.text: VS Code with the C# Dev Kit extension is a lightweight option. Visual Studio 2022 Community is more powerful, with a debugger and UI designer.

blocks.text: The classic C# program structure looks like this:
Let's go through each line:

items.text: Imports the System namespace, where the Console class lives. Without it you would have to write System.Console.
Declares the Program class — a container for code. In C#, code cannot exist outside a class.
The program's entry point. static allows calling the method without creating a Program object, void means the method returns nothing.
Console is the class for working with the console. WriteLine prints a string and adds a newline.
Curly braces define the body of the class and the method. They must come in pairs.

blocks.text: In newer .NET versions you can write it shorter: Console.WriteLine("Hello, world!"); without a class or Main — the compiler creates the entry point itself. But it is useful to understand the classic structure.

items.title: Create a project
items.text: Run dotnet new console -n Hello and change into the folder: cd Hello.

items.title: Replace the code
items.text: Open Program.cs and paste the code from the section above.

items.title: Run
items.text: Run dotnet run. “Hello, world!” will appear on the screen.

items.title: Or press F5
items.text: In Visual Studio or VS Code with the C# Dev Kit, you can launch the project with the debugger.

blocks.code:
dotnet new console -n Hello
cd Hello
dotnet run
# Hello, world!

blocks.text: Basics: data types, conditions, loops, methods, arrays and lists. Then classes, properties, interfaces, inheritance, LINQ and async/await. For games, learn Unity in parallel; for web, ASP.NET Core.

items.title: Java — a kindred language
items.text: A similar object model, but a different ecosystem.

items.title: C++ — if you need full control
items.text: Understanding memory helps in gamedev and systems code.

items.title: TypeScript — web frontend
items.text: Useful if you want to build a web interface for your C# backend.
